warmup.q: You read the first eight bytes of java/lang/Object.class from the JDK you're running. They are ca fe ba be 00 00 00 45. Which JDK is it?
options: You can't tell from the bytes
warmup.why: After the magic number CAFEBABE come the minor version (00 00) and the major version (00 45, which is 69). From Java 5 on, the Java version is major minus 44, so 69 is Java 25. JDK 21's own classes say 00 41 (65), and Java 8 is 00 34 (52).

sections.h: A class file is a byte array with a fixed layout
sections.html:
Every tool in this track reads or writes the same format. That includes javap, the verifier, Proxy, LambdaMetafactory, Byte Buddy and agents. Here is the start of java/lang/Object.class on JDK 21, printed by this section's demo:

ca fe ba be  00 00  00 41  00 7c
magic        minor  major  constant_pool_count

The magic number 0xCAFEBABE marks a class file. The major version is 0x41, which is 65, and Java 21 wrote it. From Java 5 on, the Java version is the major version minus 44. Then comes constant_pool_count, and after it the constant pool itself, the table of names and constants from lesson 2. All numbers are big-endian. DataInputStream reads them, so the first fields take four lines:

Java
DataInputStream in = new DataInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes));
int magic = in.readInt();               // u4: 0xCAFEBABE
int minor = in.readUnsignedShort();     // u2
int major = in.readUnsignedShort();     // u2: 65 = Java 21, 69 = Java 25
int poolCount = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2: entries are numbered 1 .. poolCount - 1
Kotlin
val input = DataInputStream(ByteArrayInputStream(bytes))
val magic = input.readInt()                // u4: 0xCAFEBABE
val minor = input.readUnsignedShort()      // u2
val major = input.readUnsignedShort()      // u2: 65 = Java 21, 69 = Java 25
val poolCount = input.readUnsignedShort()  // u2: entries are numbered 1 .. poolCount - 1

The constant pool is harder. Each entry starts with a one-byte tag, and the tag decides how many bytes follow: a Utf8 entry has a length, a Class entry has two bytes, a Methodref has four. A Long or Double entry takes two pool indexes, which is why lesson 2's pool had no entry 8. After the pool come the access flags, then this_class, an index that points at a Class entry, then the superclass, interfaces, fields, methods and attributes. In the lab you write this walk yourself and check it against a real class-file library.

That is the problem the ClassFile API solves. Any framework that generates or changes classes has to read and write this format exactly. The format also gains a major version with every JDK release, every six months, and sometimes new entry kinds or attributes. Until JDK 24 the JDK had no public library for it. Frameworks bundled ASM (Byte Buddy contains its own copy) and had to ship a new release for each new class-file version. The JDK carried a private copy of ASM too, and it's gone from the jdk-25-ga source tree.

try.title: Read three class-file headers
steps: Before you run anything, predict the major version of ClassFileHeader.class (built by the labs), of java.lang.Object on the JDK you're using, and of kotlin.Unit in the Kotlin standard library.
If you have both JDK 21 and JDK 25 installed, run the Java version on each: java -cp bytecode/build/classes/java/demo:bytecode/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.bytecode.l06.ClassFileHeader.

code.title: ClassFileHeader.java
code.html: package workbench.bytecode.l06; import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream; import java.io.DataInputStream; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.InputStream; import java.util.HexFormat; /** The first ten bytes of three class files: magic, version and constant pool size. */ public class ClassFileHeader { public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { show(ClassFileHeader.class); // compiled by the labs build with release 21 show(HeaderMarker.class); // compiled by kotlinc in the same build (from ClassFileHeader.kt) show(Object.class); // from the JDK you are running } static void show(Class<?> c) throws IOException { byte[] bytes; try (InputStream in = c.getResourceAsStream(c.getSimpleName() + ".class")) { bytes = in.readAllBytes(); } DataInputStream in = new DataInputStream(new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes)); int magic = in.readInt(); // u4 int minor = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2 int major = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2 int poolCount = in.readUnsignedShort(); // u2: entries are numbered 1 .. poolCount - 1 System.out.printf("%-34s %s magic=%X version=%d.%d (Java %d) pool entries=%d size=%d bytes%n", c.getName(), HexFormat.ofDelimiter(" ").formatHex(bytes, 0, 10), magic, major, minor, major - 44, poolCount - 1, bytes.length); } }

alt.title: ClassFileHeader.kt
alt.html: package workbench.bytecode.l06 import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream import java.io.DataInputStream import java.util.HexFormat /** A Kotlin class for the Java twin to read. */ class HeaderMarker /** The first ten bytes of three class files: magic, version and constant pool size. */ fun main() { show(HeaderMarker::class.java) // compiled by kotlinc in the labs build with jvmTarget 21 show(Unit::class.java) // the Kotlin standard library jar show(Any::class.java) // java.lang.Object, from the JDK you are running } private fun show(c: Class<*>) { val bytes = c.getResourceAsStream(c.simpleName + ".class")!!.use { it.readAllBytes() } val input = DataInputStream(ByteArrayInputStream(bytes)) val magic = input.readInt() // u4 val minor = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2 val major = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2 val poolCount = input.readUnsignedShort() // u2: entries are numbered 1 .. poolCount - 1 println("%-34s %s magic=%X version=%d.%d (Java %d) pool entries=%d size=%d bytes".format( c.name, HexFormat.ofDelimiter(" ").formatHex(bytes, 0, 10), magic, major, minor, major - 44, poolCount - 1, bytes.size)) }

try.expect: Every line starts with ca fe ba be. The labs' own classes (Java and Kotlin) are version=65.0 (Java 21), because the build uses release 21 and jvmTarget 21. java.lang.Object is 65 on JDK 21 and 69 on JDK 25, so the same program reports the JDK it runs on. kotlin.Unit is 52.0 (Java 8): the standard library is compiled for Java 8, so it runs everywhere.

refs.title: JVM Specification SE 25, chapter 4: The class File Format

sections.h: The ClassFile API parses bytes into an immutable model
sections.html:
The package java.lang.classfile is the JDK's own class-file library. It was a preview feature in JDK 22 (JEP 457) and JDK 23 (JEP 466), and became final in JDK 24 (JEP 484). The labs compile with release 21, so this lesson's ClassFile API code lives in single-file programs under labs/bytecode/preview/, which you run with java File.java on JDK 24 or later. On JDK 21 they fail with package java.lang.classfile does not exist.

Everything starts at ClassFile.of(). Its parse method turns bytes into a ClassModel:

Java
ClassModel cm = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes);
System.out.println(cm.thisClass().asInternalName() + " major " + cm.majorVersion());
for (MethodModel m : cm.methods()) {
    long invokes = m.code()
            .map(code -> code.elementStream().filter(e -> e instanceof InvokeInstruction).count())
            .orElse(0L);
    System.out.println(m.methodName().stringValue() + m.methodType().stringValue() + " invokes=" + invokes);
}
Kotlin
val cm = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes)
println("${cm.thisClass().asInternalName()} major ${cm.majorVersion()}")
for (m in cm.methods()) {
    val invokes = m.code()
        .map { code -> code.elementStream().filter { it is InvokeInstruction }.count() }
        .orElse(0L)
    println("${m.methodName().stringValue()}${m.methodType().stringValue()} invokes=$invokes")
}

A model is an immutable description of one part of a class file. There are models for the class, each field, each method, and each method's code. The package documentation adds two properties. A ClassModel "is inflated lazily; most parts of the classfile are not parsed until they are actually needed". So a malformed method can parse fine and throw IllegalArgumentException only when you open it.

Each model can also be read as a sequence of elements. A class's elements are its methods, fields and attributes. A method's code is a sequence of instructions, labels and other code elements. Each instruction is an object with a type you can match on, such as InvokeInstruction, ConstantInstruction or InvokeDynamicInstruction. The rest of the API is built on that: reading walks elements, building emits elements, and transforming maps elements to elements.

Names and types come back as constant-pool entries (methodName() is a Utf8Entry, which is why the code calls stringValue()). When you build, you pass symbolic descriptions from java.lang.constant, such as ClassDesc.of("FeeRule") and MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long), and the library creates the entries.

try.title: Tour lesson 2's class with the ClassFile API
steps: This needs JDK 24 or later. From labs/, make sure lesson 2's demo was built (./gradlew :bytecode:demo -Pmain=workbench.bytecode.l02.StackDemo), then run the command below. The Kotlin twin needs kotlinc running on JDK 24 or later.
Compare the constant-pool counts with the javap -v listing you read in lesson 2.
describe builds a string and calls nothing else, yet its count is 0. Before reading on: which instruction does it contain, and why didn't the filter count it?

code.title: ClassFileTour.java (JDK 24+)
code.html: // JDK 24 or later (the ClassFile API is final since JDK 24, JEP 484). From labs/: // java bytecode/preview/ClassFileTour.java [path/to/Some.class] // With no argument it reads StackDemo.class from lesson 2 (run that demo once first), // or java.lang.Integer from the running JDK if the file isn't there. import java.lang.classfile.ClassFile; import java.lang.classfile.ClassModel; import java.lang.classfile.MethodModel; import java.lang.classfile.constantpool.PoolEntry; import java.lang.classfile.instruction.InvokeInstruction; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.Map; import java.util.TreeMap; public class ClassFileTour { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { Path p = Path.of(args.length > 0 ? args[0] : "bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.class"); byte[] bytes = Files.exists(p) ? Files.readAllBytes(p) : Integer.class.getResourceAsStream("Integer.class").readAllBytes(); // 1. parse: an immutable model, inflated lazily as you ask for parts ClassModel cm = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes); System.out.println(cm.thisClass().asInternalName() + " extends " + cm.superclass().map(c -> c.asInternalName()).orElse("-") + ", major " + cm.majorVersion()); // 2. the constant pool, counted by kind of entry Map<String, Integer> kinds = new TreeMap<>(); for (PoolEntry e : cm.constantPool()) { kinds.merge(e.getClass().getInterfaces()[0].getSimpleName(), 1, Integer::sum); } System.out.println("constant pool: " + kinds); // 3. methods, and the invoke instructions inside each one for (MethodModel m : cm.methods()) { long invokes = m.code() .map(code -> code.elementStream().filter(e -> e instanceof InvokeInstruction).count()) .orElse(0L); System.out.println(" " + m.methodName().stringValue() + m.methodType().stringValue() + " invokes=" + invokes); } } }

From labs/: // kotlinc bytecode/preview/ClassFileTour.kt -jvm-target 21 -include-runtime -d build/cftour.jar // java -jar build/cftour.jar [path/to/Some.class] // With no argument it reads StackDemo.class from lesson 2, or java.lang.Integer from the JDK. import java.lang.classfile.ClassFile import java.lang.classfile.instruction.InvokeInstruction import java.nio.file.Files import java.nio.file.Path fun main(args: Array<String>) { val p = Path.of(args.firstOrNull() ?: "bytecode/build/classes/java/demo/workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo.class") val bytes = if (Files.exists(p)) Files.readAllBytes(p) else Int::class.javaObjectType.getResourceAsStream("Integer.class")!!.readAllBytes() // 1. parse: an immutable model, inflated lazily as you ask for parts val cm = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes) println("${cm.thisClass().asInternalName()} extends ${cm.superclass().map { it.asInternalName() }.orElse("-")}, major ${cm.majorVersion()}") // 2. the constant pool, counted by kind of entry val kinds = cm.constantPool().groupingBy { it.javaClass.interfaces[0].simpleName }.eachCount().toSortedMap() println("constant pool: $kinds") // 3. methods, and the invoke instructions inside each one for (m in cm.methods()) { val invokes = m.code().map { code -> code.elementStream().filter { it is InvokeInstruction }.count() }.orElse(0L) println(" ${m.methodName().stringValue()}${m.methodType().stringValue()} invokes=$invokes") } }

try.expect: workbench/bytecode/l02/StackDemo extends java/lang/Object, major 65, a pool with Utf8Entry=43, LongEntry=2 (10000 and 125000) and one InvokeDynamicEntry, then four methods: <init>()V invokes=1, feeMinor(JI)J invokes=0, describe(...) invokes=0 and main(...) invokes=3. describe contains an invokedynamic, which the API models as InvokeDynamicInstruction, a separate type from InvokeInstruction.

sections.h: Builders write a class from lambdas, and verify checks it before you load it
sections.html:
To generate a class you don't create builder objects yourself. You pass lambdas, and the library hands each one the builder for that level: a ClassBuilder for the class, a CodeBuilder for a method body. The CodeBuilder has one method per instruction, so a method body reads like the javap listings from lesson 2:

Java
byte[] feeRule = ClassFile.of().build(ClassDesc.of("FeeRule"), clb -> clb
        .withFlags(ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_FINAL)
        .withMethodBody("fee", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC,
                cob -> cob
                        .lload(0)          // the amount, slots 0 and 1
                        .ldc(290L)         // basis points
                        .lmul()
                        .ldc(10_000L)
                        .ldiv()
                        .lreturn()));
Class<?> c = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(feeRule);   // load it next to this class
Kotlin
val feeRule = ClassFile.of().build(ClassDesc.of("FeeRule")) { clb ->
    clb.withFlags(ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC or ClassFile.ACC_FINAL)
    clb.withMethodBody("fee", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC or ClassFile.ACC_STATIC) { cob ->
        cob.lload(0)                       // the amount, slots 0 and 1
            .loadConstant(290L)            // basis points (Kotlin: see below)
            .lmul()
            .loadConstant(10_000L)
            .ldiv()
            .lreturn()
    }
}
val c = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(feeRule)            // load it next to this class

fee(125000) returns 3625, the fee you computed by hand in lesson 2. MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass loads the bytes as a class in the same package and loader as the calling class.

The builder writes what you tell it to, including nonsense. A method declared to return int that pushes a String builds without complaint. Lesson 1 showed what happens when you load such a class: defineClass can succeed and the VerifyError comes later. ClassFile.of().verify(bytes) runs the verifier's checks on the bytes before any of that, and returns a list of errors:

verify(FeeRule): []
verify(Broken):  [java.lang.VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack in Broken::answer() @2
                  (integer_type is not assignable from java/lang/String)]

Kotlin has one trap here. ldc takes a java.lang.constant.ConstantDesc, and Java's String and Long implement that interface. Kotlin's String and Long types don't show it, so cob.ldc("forty-two") doesn't compile in Kotlin. Use loadConstant(310L), which has overloads for primitives, or pass a constant-pool entry: cob.ldc(cob.constantPool().stringEntry("forty-two")).

try.title: Build, verify, then break it
steps: On JDK 24 or later, run ClassFileForge from labs/ (command below), or build and run the Kotlin twin.
Read the first three lines: the size of the generated class, its verify result, the fee, and the verifier's message for Broken.
In the fee body, delete the .ldiv() line and predict what verify(feeRule) reports. Run it again.

code.title: ClassFileForge.java (JDK 24+)
code.html: // JDK 24 or later (the ClassFile API is final since JDK 24, JEP 484). From labs/: // java bytecode/preview/ClassFileForge.java // Builds a class from scratch, verifies a broken one, then transforms the first. import java.lang.classfile.ClassFile; import java.lang.classfile.ClassModel; import java.lang.classfile.ClassTransform; import java.lang.classfile.CodeTransform; import java.lang.classfile.MethodModel; import java.lang.classfile.instruction.ConstantInstruction; import java.lang.constant.ClassDesc; import java.lang.constant.MethodTypeDesc; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles; import static java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_String; import static java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_int; import static java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_long; import static java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_void; public class ClassFileForge { public static void main(String[] args) throws Throwable { ClassFile cf = ClassFile.of(); // 1. build: a class with fee(long) = amount * 290 / 10_000 and a debug method byte[] feeRule = cf.build(ClassDesc.of("FeeRule"), clb -> clb .withFlags(ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_FINAL) .withMethodBody("fee", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC, cob -> cob .lload(0) // push the amount (slots 0 and 1) .ldc(290L) // push the rate in basis points .lmul() .ldc(10_000L) .ldiv() .lreturn()) .withMethodBody("debugTrace", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_void, CD_String), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC, cob -> cob .return_())); System.out.println("built FeeRule: " + feeRule.length + " bytes, verify errors " + cf.verify(feeRule)); Class<?> c1 = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(feeRule); System.out.println("FeeRule.fee(125000) = " + c1.getMethod("fee", long.class).invoke(null, 125_000L)); // 2. verify before you load: an int method that returns a String byte[] broken = cf.build(ClassDesc.of("Broken"), clb -> clb .withMethodBody("answer", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_int), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC, cob -> cob.ldc("forty-two").ireturn())); System.out.println("verify(Broken): " + cf.verify(broken)); // 3. transform: drop debug methods and change the 290 constant to 310, as a new class FeeRuleV2 ClassModel model = cf.parse(feeRule); CodeTransform newRate = (cob, element) -> { if (element instanceof ConstantInstruction ci && Long.valueOf(290L).equals(ci.constantValue())) { cob.ldc(310L); // replace this element } else { cob.with(element); // pass everything else through unchanged } }; ClassTransform transform = ClassTransform .dropping(e -> e instanceof MethodModel m && m.methodName().stringValue().startsWith("debug")) .andThen(ClassTransform.transformingMethodBodies(newRate)); byte[] v2 = cf.transformClass(model, ClassDesc.of("FeeRuleV2"), transform); Class<?> c2 = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(v2); System.out.println("FeeRuleV2 methods " + cf.parse(v2).methods().stream().map(m -> m.methodName().stringValue()).toList() + ", fee(125000) = " + c2.getMethod("fee", long.class).invoke(null, 125_000L)); } }

try.expect: built FeeRule: 197 bytes, verify errors [], FeeRule.fee(125000) = 3625, and verify(Broken): [java.lang.VerifyError: Bad type on operand stack in Broken::answer() @2 (integer_type is not assignable from java/lang/String)]. Without ldiv, two longs are still on the stack at lreturn. That's legal for the verifier, which only checks the type on top, so verify reports no error and fee(125000) returns 10000 (the last value pushed). The verifier proves the code is type-safe, not that it's right.

sections.h: A transform is a flatMap over elements
sections.html:
Changing an existing class is where the element model pays off. The package documentation puts it in one sentence: "Transformation can be viewed as a 'flatMap' operation on the sequence of elements; for every element, we could pass it through unchanged, drop it, or replace it with one or more elements."

A ClassTransform sees class elements, and a CodeTransform sees the instructions of one method. Inside a transform you hand each element to the builder: builder.with(element) passes it through, calling nothing drops it, and calling other builder methods replaces it. This one drops every debug... method and changes the rate constant in every method body:

Java
CodeTransform newRate = (cob, element) -> {
    if (element instanceof ConstantInstruction ci && Long.valueOf(290L).equals(ci.constantValue())) {
        cob.ldc(310L);            // replace
    } else {
        cob.with(element);        // pass through
    }
};
ClassTransform transform = ClassTransform
        .dropping(e -> e instanceof MethodModel m && m.methodName().stringValue().startsWith("debug"))
        .andThen(ClassTransform.transformingMethodBodies(newRate));
byte[] v2 = cf.transformClass(cf.parse(feeRule), ClassDesc.of("FeeRuleV2"), transform);
Kotlin
val newRate = CodeTransform { cob, element ->
    if (element is ConstantInstruction && element.constantValue().equals(290L)) {
        cob.loadConstant(310L)    // replace
    } else {
        cob.with(element)         // pass through
    }
}
val transform = ClassTransform
    .dropping { it is MethodModel && it.methodName().stringValue().startsWith("debug") }
    .andThen(ClassTransform.transformingMethodBodies(newRate))
val v2 = cf.transformClass(cf.parse(feeRule), ClassDesc.of("FeeRuleV2"), transform)

The result, FeeRuleV2, has only fee, and fee(125000) returns 3875. Everything the transform passed through is copied, and that's also the default: a transform that does nothing reproduces the class.

The JDK writes its own generated classes with this API. ProxyGenerator switched from the internal ASM to java.lang.classfile in JDK 23, and the lambda spinner InnerClassLambdaMetafactory in JDK 24. So the $Proxy0 from lesson 4 and the $$Lambda classes from lesson 3 are built by the code you just ran.

Who should use it? Tools that only need to run on JDK 24 and later can drop their ASM dependency, because the API always matches the JDK it runs on. Libraries that must support older JDKs can't do that. Byte Buddy, whose regular jar targets Java 8 and whose -jdk5 jar targets Java 5, keeps its bundled ASM and bridges to the ClassFile API when it's there (release notes for 1.16.0: "Include support for JDK Class File API"). Lesson 7 runs transforms on classes that are already loaded, which is what agents do.

try.title: Write your own transform
steps: Run ClassFileForge again and read the last line.
Change the code transform so it also turns 10_000L into 1_000L, without touching the 290 branch. Predict the new FeeRuleV2.fee(125000) before you run it.
Remove the .andThen(...) part, keeping only dropping. Which line of the output changes?

code.title: ClassFileForge.java (JDK 24+)
code.html: // JDK 24 or later (the ClassFile API is final since JDK 24, JEP 484). From labs/: // java bytecode/preview/ClassFileForge.java // Builds a class from scratch, verifies a broken one, then transforms the first. import java.lang.classfile.ClassFile; import java.lang.classfile.ClassModel; import java.lang.classfile.ClassTransform; import java.lang.classfile.CodeTransform; import java.lang.classfile.MethodModel; import java.lang.classfile.instruction.ConstantInstruction; import java.lang.constant.ClassDesc; import java.lang.constant.MethodTypeDesc; import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles; import static java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_String; import static java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_int; import static java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_long; import static java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_void; public class ClassFileForge { public static void main(String[] args) throws Throwable { ClassFile cf = ClassFile.of(); // 1. build: a class with fee(long) = amount * 290 / 10_000 and a debug method byte[] feeRule = cf.build(ClassDesc.of("FeeRule"), clb -> clb .withFlags(ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_FINAL) .withMethodBody("fee", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC, cob -> cob .lload(0) // push the amount (slots 0 and 1) .ldc(290L) // push the rate in basis points .lmul() .ldc(10_000L) .ldiv() .lreturn()) .withMethodBody("debugTrace", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_void, CD_String), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC, cob -> cob .return_())); System.out.println("built FeeRule: " + feeRule.length + " bytes, verify errors " + cf.verify(feeRule)); Class<?> c1 = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(feeRule); System.out.println("FeeRule.fee(125000) = " + c1.getMethod("fee", long.class).invoke(null, 125_000L)); // 2. verify before you load: an int method that returns a String byte[] broken = cf.build(ClassDesc.of("Broken"), clb -> clb .withMethodBody("answer", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_int), ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC | ClassFile.ACC_STATIC, cob -> cob.ldc("forty-two").ireturn())); System.out.println("verify(Broken): " + cf.verify(broken)); // 3. transform: drop debug methods and change the 290 constant to 310, as a new class FeeRuleV2 ClassModel model = cf.parse(feeRule); CodeTransform newRate = (cob, element) -> { if (element instanceof ConstantInstruction ci && Long.valueOf(290L).equals(ci.constantValue())) { cob.ldc(310L); // replace this element } else { cob.with(element); // pass everything else through unchanged } }; ClassTransform transform = ClassTransform .dropping(e -> e instanceof MethodModel m && m.methodName().stringValue().startsWith("debug")) .andThen(ClassTransform.transformingMethodBodies(newRate)); byte[] v2 = cf.transformClass(model, ClassDesc.of("FeeRuleV2"), transform); Class<?> c2 = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(v2); System.out.println("FeeRuleV2 methods " + cf.parse(v2).methods().stream().map(m -> m.methodName().stringValue()).toList() + ", fee(125000) = " + c2.getMethod("fee", long.class).invoke(null, 125_000L)); } }

alt.title: ClassFileForge.kt (JDK 24+)
alt.html: // JDK 24 or later, with kotlinc running on that JDK. From labs/: // kotlinc bytecode/preview/ClassFileForge.kt -jvm-target 21 -include-runtime -d build/cfforge.jar // java -jar build/cfforge.jar // Builds a class from scratch, verifies a broken one, then transforms the first. import java.lang.classfile.ClassFile import java.lang.classfile.ClassTransform import java.lang.classfile.CodeTransform import java.lang.classfile.MethodModel import java.lang.classfile.instruction.ConstantInstruction import java.lang.constant.ClassDesc import java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_String import java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_int import java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_long import java.lang.constant.ConstantDescs.CD_void import java.lang.constant.MethodTypeDesc import java.lang.invoke.MethodHandles fun main() { val cf = ClassFile.of() val static = ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC or ClassFile.ACC_STATIC // 1. build: a class with fee(long) = amount * 290 / 10_000 and a debug method val feeRule = cf.build(ClassDesc.of("FeeRule")) { clb -> clb.withFlags(ClassFile.ACC_PUBLIC or ClassFile.ACC_FINAL) clb.withMethodBody("fee", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_long, CD_long), static) { cob -> cob.lload(0) // push the amount (slots 0 and 1) .loadConstant(290L) // push the rate in basis points (ldc2_w) .lmul() .loadConstant(10_000L) .ldiv() .lreturn() } clb.withMethodBody("debugTrace", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_void, CD_String), static) { cob -> cob.return_() } } println("built FeeRule: ${feeRule.size} bytes, verify errors ${cf.verify(feeRule)}") val c1 = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(feeRule) println("FeeRule.fee(125000) = ${c1.getMethod("fee", Long::class.javaPrimitiveType).invoke(null, 125_000L)}") // 2. verify before you load: an int method that returns a String val broken = cf.build(ClassDesc.of("Broken")) { clb -> clb.withMethodBody("answer", MethodTypeDesc.of(CD_int), static) { cob -> // Kotlin's String type doesn't expose Java's ConstantDesc, so pass a constant-pool entry cob.ldc(cob.constantPool().stringEntry("forty-two")).ireturn() } } println("verify(Broken): ${cf.verify(broken)}") // 3. transform: drop debug methods and change the 290 constant to 310, as a new class FeeRuleV2 val newRate = CodeTransform { cob, element -> if (element is ConstantInstruction && element.constantValue().equals(290L)) { cob.loadConstant(310L) // replace this element } else { cob.with(element) // pass everything else through unchanged } } val transform = ClassTransform .dropping { it is MethodModel && it.methodName().stringValue().startsWith("debug") } .andThen(ClassTransform.transformingMethodBodies(newRate)) val v2 = cf.transformClass(cf.parse(feeRule), ClassDesc.of("FeeRuleV2"), transform) val c2 = MethodHandles.lookup().defineClass(v2) println("FeeRuleV2 methods ${cf.parse(v2).methods().map { it.methodName().stringValue() }}, " + "fee(125000) = ${c2.getMethod("fee", Long::class.javaPrimitiveType).invoke(null, 125_000L)}") }

try.expect: Before your change: FeeRuleV2 methods [fee], fee(125000) = 3875. With both constants replaced: 125000 x 310 / 1000 = 38750. With only dropping, FeeRuleV2 still loses debugTrace, but fee keeps the 290 constant and returns 3625 again.

analogy: A class file is a filled-in form with a strict layout: boxes in a fixed order, a numbered glossary at the front (the constant pool), and every later box that needs a name writes a glossary number instead. Reading by hand means walking the glossary line by line, remembering that some entries take two lines. The ClassFile API is a clerk who reads the form into a folder of typed cards (models and elements), lets you hand back a new folder card by card (builders), and copies a form while you say "keep, drop, or replace" for each card (transforms). The analogy breaks at checking: a clerk would notice a nonsense answer. The builder writes whatever you hand it, and only verify asks whether the result is type-safe, never whether it's correct.
world: You meet the class-file format first in a deploy failure: UnsupportedClassVersionError: ... class file version 69.0, this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file versions up to 65.0. A library or a module was compiled for JDK 25 and your service image still runs JDK 21. Reading the header of every class in the jars (the lab's header does it) finds the culprit in a minute. Later you may write a build-time check that no class in the payments service references a banned class, such as java.util.Random in token generation. That check is the lab's referencedClasses over every class file, or twenty lines of ClassFile API code on JDK 25.
mistake: The common mistake is treating verify (or a class that loads) as proof the generated code is right. The verifier checks types and stack shapes: that lreturn finds a long, that a method returns what its descriptor promises. A builder that leaves an extra value on the stack, pushes the wrong constant or forgets a division can still pass, as the ldiv experiment showed. People make the mistake because a VerifyError feels like the compiler's error checking. The fix is to test generated classes like any code: load them, call them with known inputs, and assert the results, as the lab's tests do against an independent reader.

compare.title: Reading a class's name in Java and Kotlin, by hand and with the API

java.title: ThisClass.java
java.html: // by hand (any JDK): walk the pool, then read this_class static String thisClass(byte[] bytes) { return ClassFileFacts.thisClass(bytes); // the lab's DataInputStream walk } // with the ClassFile API (JDK 24+) static String thisClassWithApi(byte[] bytes) { return ClassFile.of().parse(bytes).thisClass().asInternalName(); }

kotlin.title: ThisClass.kt
kotlin.html: // by hand (any JDK): walk the pool, then read this_class fun thisClass(bytes: ByteArray): String = ClassFileFacts.thisClass(bytes) // the lab's DataInputStream walk // with the ClassFile API (JDK 24+) fun thisClassWithApi(bytes: ByteArray): String = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes).thisClass().asInternalName()

compare.note: Same bytes, same answer, and the API version is one line because the library does the pool walk for you, lazily. The language differences are small but real. Kotlin calls the API through ordinary SAM conversion for its Consumer and CodeTransform parameters, and uses or instead of | for access flags. Kotlin's mapped String and Long types don't expose Java's ConstantDesc, so ldc("...") needs a constant-pool entry or loadConstant instead. Compiling Kotlin against the API also needs kotlinc to run on (or point -jdk-home at) JDK 24 or later, whatever -jvm-target you choose.

worked.title: Find the jar that broke the deploy

steps.say: The payments service starts on JDK 21 and dies at once. Which part of the message tells you what to look for?
steps.code:
Error: LinkageError occurred while loading main class com.acme.fx.RateTable
    java.lang.UnsupportedClassVersionError: com/acme/fx/RateTable has been compiled by a more
    recent version of the Java Runtime (class file version 69.0), this version of the Java Runtime
    only recognizes class file versions up to 65.0

steps.say: Class file version 69.0 is Java 25 (69 - 44). Something in the image was compiled for JDK 25. Here only one class is named, but a jar can mix versions, so check every class. Read each entry's header, with the lab's code.
steps.code: try (JarFile jar = new JarFile(path.toFile())) { jar.stream() .filter(e -> e.getName().endsWith(".class")) .forEach(e -> { try (InputStream in = jar.getInputStream(e)) { // 1. read magic, minor, major from the first 10 bytes ClassFileFacts.Header h = ClassFileFacts.header(in.readNBytes(10)); // 2. report anything newer than the runtime if (h.major() > 65) System.out.println(e.getName() + " -> Java " + ClassFileFacts.javaVersion(h.major())); } catch (IOException ex) { throw new UncheckedIOException(ex); } }); }

alt.html: JarFile(path.toFile()).use { jar -> jar.stream() .filter { it.name.endsWith(".class") } .forEach { e -> // 1. read magic, minor, major from the first 10 bytes val h = jar.getInputStream(e).use { ClassFileFacts.header(it.readNBytes(10)) } // 2. report anything newer than the runtime if (h.major() > 65) println("${e.name} -> Java ${ClassFileFacts.javaVersion(h.major())}") } }

steps.say: Two caveats. A multi-release jar keeps newer classes under META-INF/versions/25/, and those are allowed: the JVM only loads them on JDK 25. So skip that prefix, or you'll get false alarms. And module-info.class has a version too. When the culprit is your own module, the fix is in the build: compile with --release 21 (Gradle: options.release.set(21)) and jvmTarget = 21 for Kotlin, as the labs do, so the compilers also refuse JDK 22+ APIs.

lab.title: Read the constant pool by hand
steps: Run the tests once. All seven fail. Read the class-file layout and the tag table in the Javadoc of ClassFileFacts.

Write header: wrap the bytes in a DataInputStream, read the int magic and throw IllegalArgumentException (with "magic" in the message) if it isn't 0xCAFEBABE, then read three unsigned shorts. Write javaVersion as major - 44, rejecting anything below 49.

Write a private pool walk: for i from 1 to count - 1, read the tag and either keep the value (readUTF() for tag 1, the name index for tag 7) or skip the right number of bytes. After a tag 5 or 6, add one to i.
Write referencedClasses with the walk: the Utf8 string at each Class entry's name index. Write thisClass: after the walk, read access_flags, then this_class, and look up its name.
Run the tests until all seven pass. The expected answers come from ASM, so a pass means your reader agrees with a production library on Java, Kotlin and JDK classes.
hints: A wrong byte count anywhere in the walk shifts everything after it, so the symptom is usually unknown constant pool tag far from the bug. Check the table entry for the last tag you handled.
DataInputStream.readUTF() reads a two-byte length and then the bytes in the class file's own "modified UTF-8". That's exactly a Utf8 entry, so you don't decode anything yourself.
Forgetting the extra index after Long and Double passes for some classes and fails for Fixture, which has both.

drill.title: The constant pool walk from memory
drill.prompt: Close the page and the lab. Write the loop that walks a constant pool with a DataInputStream, given count. Handle Utf8, Class, the fixed-size entries and the two-index entries. Then check: which tags take two pool indexes, and which entry has a 3-byte body?

answer.html: for (int i = 1; i < count; i++) { // index 0 is never used int tag = in.readUnsignedByte(); switch (tag) { case 1 -> utf8[i] = in.readUTF(); // Utf8: u2 length + bytes case 7 -> classNameIndex[i] = in.readUnsignedShort(); case 8, 16, 19, 20 -> in.skipBytes(2); // String, MethodType, Module, Package case 15 -> in.skipBytes(3); // MethodHandle: u1 kind + u2 index case 3, 4, 9, 10, 11, 12, 17, 18 -> in.skipBytes(4); case 5, 6 -> { in.skipBytes(8); i++; } // Long, Double: two indexes default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("tag " + tag + " at " + i); } }

alt.html: var i = 1 // index 0 is never used while (i < count) { when (val tag = input.readUnsignedByte()) { 1 -> utf8[i] = input.readUTF() // Utf8: u2 length + bytes 7 -> classNameIndex[i] = input.readUnsignedShort() 8, 16, 19, 20 -> input.skipBytes(2) // String, MethodType, Module, Package 15 -> input.skipBytes(3) // MethodHandle: u1 kind + u2 index 3, 4, 9, 10, 11, 12, 17, 18 -> input.skipBytes(4) 5, 6 -> { input.skipBytes(8); i++ } // Long, Double: two indexes else -> throw IllegalArgumentException("tag $tag at $i") } i++ }

recap: A class file starts with CAFEBABE, minor and major version (Java version = major - 44 from Java 5 on: 65 is 21, 69 is 25), then the constant pool.
Pool entries start with a tag that fixes their size; Long and Double take two indexes. this_class comes right after the pool and the access flags.
The ClassFile API (java.lang.classfile) was preview in JDK 22 and 23 and became final in JDK 24 (JEP 484). Labs on release 21 can't use it, so its code runs as JDK 25 single-file programs.
ClassFile.of().parse gives a lazy, immutable ClassModel; models are also sequences of elements, such as methods or instructions.
build takes builder lambdas, verify checks type safety before loading (not correctness), and transformClass maps elements: pass with with, drop by doing nothing, or replace.
The JDK builds proxies (since 23) and lambdas (since 24) with it. Libraries that support old JDKs, like Byte Buddy, keep their own ASM and bridge to it.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why a hand-written constant-pool walk is fiddly, what the ClassFile API's model, builder and transform each give you, and why the API's arrival in JDK 24 matters for frameworks.
explain.answer: A class file stores every name and constant in a numbered pool, and each entry's size depends on its tag. You must handle every tag, and Long and Double take two indexes, so one wrong count misreads everything after it. The ClassFile API does that walk for you. parse gives an immutable, lazily parsed model of the class, its methods and their code, which you can read as sequences of typed elements. build takes lambdas that receive builders with one method per instruction, and verify checks type safety before you load the result. transformClass copies a class while you decide, element by element, to pass it through, drop it or replace it. Before JDK 24 the JDK had no public library, so frameworks bundled ASM and needed a new release for each class-file version. The API always matches the JDK it runs on, and the JDK now builds its own proxies and lambdas with it.

deeper.html:
Three details from the API's documentation and this track's runs.

Models are lazy, and that can surprise you. parse reads little more than the header. A method's code is inflated when you ask for it, so a malformed method can parse fine and fail with IllegalArgumentException later, when you iterate its elements. If you run untrusted or generated bytes through the API, iterate or verify them up front.

The ClassFile API and Byte Buddy are complements. Byte Buddy works at the level of types and methods (subclass this, intercept those methods with that delegate), and it runs on JDK 8. The ClassFile API works at the level of the class file (these instructions, that constant), and it needs JDK 24. Byte Buddy's README says that "as of 1.17.0, support will extend to new Java versions unless previously unknown class file features are discovered. This is possible through Byte Buddy's support of the Class File API." So on a new JDK, Byte Buddy can lean on the JDK's own reader and writer.

ConstantPool is Iterable<PoolEntry>, not a collection, so Java needs StreamSupport to stream it, while Kotlin's Iterable extensions work directly:

Java
// JDK 24+: every Class entry a class references, with the API
Set<String> names = StreamSupport.stream(ClassFile.of().parse(bytes).constantPool().spliterator(), false)
        .filter(e -> e instanceof ClassEntry)
        .map(e -> ((ClassEntry) e).asInternalName())
        .collect(Collectors.toCollection(TreeSet::new));
Kotlin
// JDK 24+: every Class entry a class references, with the API
val names = ClassFile.of().parse(bytes).constantPool()
    .filterIsInstance<ClassEntry>()
    .map { it.asInternalName() }
    .toSortedSet()
